front.title: Protocol Poker handoff
front.copy: Flip to sync secrets: server is the dealer; clients see only their hand. Use low-latency channels for fair play.

back.title: Ready-made board copy
back.copy: Server holds the deck and streams lane-specific views. In replies, cite one concrete example.
back.fact: TED (Celeste Headlee): Listen for ideas — not pauses.

front.title: Solo practice
front.copy: Draft a 25-word reply to a peer and end with a single invitational question.

back.title: Fact + flip
back.copy: Short, specific invites increase engagement; name one example or source.
back.fact: Study: Brief prompts raise reply rates in peer groups.

front.title: Audience-first opener
front.copy: In two lines say who benefits and the action you want. Keep verbs active.

back.title: Anchor & ask
back.copy: Anchor with one evidence phrase then invite critique: 'Evidence X suggests Y. What would you question?'
back.fact: TED: Ask for stories, not stats, to get richer answers.

front.title: Color field check-in
front.copy: Pick an oil-foil color for today’s mood and name one micro-scene it lights up.

back.title: Scene partner
back.copy: Ask for one sensory detail and pause; sensory details beat yes/no replies.
back.fact: TED: Sensory prompts produce richer responses.

front.title: Evidence anchor
front.copy: State one claim and add one concrete piece of evidence (data, quote or quick example).

back.title: Keep it tight
back.copy: Name the source and one takeaway; short citations increase credibility.
back.fact: Practice: concise attribution improves perceived reliability.

front.title: Story prompt
front.copy: Ask a peer for one brief story connected to the topic (one paragraph max).

back.title: Why stories work
back.copy: Stories create concrete details others can respond to; ask for one sensory anchor.
back.fact: Research: Stories are more memorable than abstract claims.

front.title: Question framing
front.copy: Rewrite a vague prompt into a precise question that asks for an example or reason.

back.title: Edit for clarity
back.copy: Specific questions reduce noise and invite evidence-based replies.
back.fact: Practice: Clear questions consistently get better peer responses.

front.title: Peer feedback
front.copy: Give one praise plus one specific suggestion (no more than two sentences).

back.title: Sandwich method
back.copy: Praise + suggestion helps peers listen and reduces defensiveness.
back.fact: Practice: Balanced feedback increases adoption of suggestions.

front.title: Cite habit
front.copy: When you claim something add 'According to [source]' or 'In my experience…' and one detail.

back.title: Small citation
back.copy: One short attribution improves trust and points readers to follow-up material.
back.fact: Research: Brief citations increase perceived reliability.

front.title: Active listening
front.copy: Paraphrase a peer's point in one sentence before adding your view.

back.title: Listen for ideas
back.copy: Paraphrase shows you understood and helps others refine their thinking.
back.fact: TED (Celeste Headlee): Listen for ideas, not pauses.

front.title: Challenge kindly
front.copy: Pose one constructive challenge: 'Have you considered X? If so, how does it affect Y?'

back.title: Constructive challenge
back.copy: Frame questions to invite deeper thinking, not to disprove.
back.fact: Socratic questioning fosters exploration without personal attack.

front.title: Reflection prompt
front.copy: Name one thing you learned today and one small change you'll try this week.

back.title: Practice change
back.copy: Small commitments increase follow-through; write one sentence to make it real.
back.fact: Research: Reflection plus action improves retention.
